text: Gather all the partial derivatives of a function into one vector and you get the gradient. It has a remarkable property: at every point, it points in the direction in which the function increases fastest, and its length tells you how steep that climb is.

Look at the function from above, as a contour map, like the lines on a hiking map that join points of equal height. For a round bowl, the contours are circles, and at each point the gradient is an arrow pointing straight outwards, uphill, crossing the contour line at a right angle.

Why is that the steepest direction? The slope in the direction of a unit arrow u is the dot product of the gradient with u, because each partial derivative contributes in proportion to how much of u points along its own axis. A dot product with a fixed arrow is largest when u points the same way as that arrow, so the steepest direction is the gradient itself, and the steepest slope is its length.

The same dot product explains the right angle. Walking along a contour line keeps your height constant, so the slope in that direction is zero, and a zero dot product means the two arrows are perpendicular. That is why the gradient always crosses the contour lines at a right angle.

Turn the arrow around, and minus the gradient is the direction of steepest descent. Gradient descent is a hiker in fog, who cannot see the valley but can feel the slope underfoot: take a small step against the gradient, measure the slope again, and repeat. In a long, narrow valley the steps zigzag from wall to wall, which hints at why we will later want cleverer optimisers.

The size of each step is set by a number called the learning rate. If it is too small, the hiker crawls and training takes forever; if it is too large, each step overshoots the valley floor and can land higher up the far side than where it began.

Training a language model is this same walk in a landscape with billions of dimensions, where the height is the loss on a batch of text, and every step moves each weight a little way against its own partial derivative. Next, we meet Jacobians, which handle functions whose output is a whole vector rather than a single number.
